readingInstruction: Read 2 Samuel 8:1-10:19. David’s kingdom reaches its height, and he shows kindness to Mephibosheth. Notice what David does with the covenant love he has received.
settingTheScene: After the covenant of chapter 7, the narrative shows the LORD giving David victory on every side. Chapter 8 summarizes his conquests and his administration. Chapter 9 turns from war to mercy, as David seeks out any survivor of Saul’s house to show kindness for Jonathan’s sake. Chapter 10 returns to war with the Ammonites and Arameans. This is the high point of David’s reign.
observation: “And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went” (8:6, 14).
“So David reigned over all Israel. And David administered justice and equity to all his people” (8:15).
David asks, “Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him the kindness of God?” (9:3).
Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, is crippled in both feet and living in Lo-debar (9:3-5).
“Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always” (9:7).
Mephibosheth bows and says, “What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I am?” (9:8).
“So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate always at the king’s table. Now he was lame in both his feet” (9:13).
Joab says, “Be of good courage, and let us be courageous for the sake of our people, and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him” (10:12).
interpretation:
Chapter 8 is a record of success, and it is framed by the repeated phrase, “The LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.” David’s reign is blessed because God is with him. He also dedicates the plunder to the LORD (8:11). The chapter closes with a summary of his administration, and with the key statement that he “administered justice and equity to all his people.” A king’s greatness is measured by his justice.

Chapter 9 is the gem of the section. It is a story of grace. Saul’s family was David’s enemy. Under the customs of the time, a new king would eliminate the old dynasty’s heirs. Instead, David asks, “Is there anyone left that I may show the kindness of God?” The phrase “kindness of God” means covenant faithfulness (the Hebrew word is the one translated “steadfast love”). He is acting out of a promise he made to Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:14-17).

Mephibosheth is a picture of every sinner. He was lame in both feet, hiding in a place called Lo-debar (“no pasture”), thinking of himself as a dead dog. He expected death. Instead, he is called, brought to the king’s table, given land, and treated as one of the king’s sons. “You shall eat at my table always.” He did nothing to earn it. He was invited because of what the king promised to another.

The scene ends with a line that is easy to miss: “Now he was lame in both his feet.” His condition did not change. He was seated at the king’s table with his disability intact. Grace does not require us to be healed before we are welcomed.

Chapter 10 returns to war and shows the other side of the king. But David is no longer the man who fears. He trusts the LORD for the result.
connection: The story of Mephibosheth is a picture of the gospel. We were far from the King, crippled by sin, and expecting judgment. But for the sake of the Son, we are brought near and seated at the table (Ephesians 2:13; Luke 22:29-30). Jesus invited the lame and the poor to his banquet (Luke 14:13-23). Revelation 19:9 speaks of the marriage supper of the Lamb. Titus 3:4-5 speaks of the kindness of God our Savior.
application:
Think of yourself as Mephibosheth. Let the picture of being brought to the table sink in.

Ask who in your life needs “the kindness of God” from you, someone who expects nothing.

Remember that you do not have to be fixed before you come to Jesus.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for his kindness to you, shown for the sake of his Son.
Ask him to teach you to show that kindness to someone who cannot repay it.
Thank him for a seat at his table.
